tagline: Bridging Geology, Microbial Ecology, and Human History Across Borders.
homeIntro:
Earth and life sciences do not exist in a vacuum—they unfold in the context of their observer—humanity. Our histories, languages, and cultures make the acquisition and dissemination of scientific knowledge possible. Additionally, it is both human appreciation for knowledge, and our ability to use it to benefit and inspire others, that makes this knowledge meaningful.

From climbing the sandstone cliffs of Suesca and experiencing local hospitality in Bogotá, Colombia, to presenting undergraduate scientific research in Reykjavík, Iceland, my time in the UF International Scholars Program shaped my mission: to pair geobiological inquiry with tangible cross-cultural service in an effort to make the world a better place.
aboutBio:
My name is Holden, and I'm a senior at the University of Florida, double-majoring in Geology and Microbiology & Cell Science with a minor in History. I aim to understand the world as best as I can, whether that be through testing out new theories and instruments in the lab, interpreting geological structures in the field, or meeting people in a completely new place. I aim to pursue astrobiology for my PhD, where I hope to work with cold-loving microbes in Antarctica. However, I also want to make an impact on others through science communication, so my future discoveries are not just for my isolated benefit, but rather help others learn to love science and chase the best version of themselves.

Outside the lab, you can find me in another lab, the gym, triathalon training, doing Duolingo, hiking and canoeing, spending time with friends and family, or just lounging around. After graduation, I aim to work for the planetary exploration technology startup, IMPRESS Spaceworks Co., before going into my PhD, doing some international volunteering along the way.
scientificLens: I aim to achieve an in-depth understanding of how microbes interact with their geologic environments and the geochemical signatures they leave behind. In my graduate studies, I will use this knowledge to advance the field of astrobiology by studying how pyschrophiles' unique adaptations facilitate their survival in frigid, alien environments.
humanitiesLens: I came into college as a History major, and still have a deep appreciation for the story of how we got where we are. I got into science because I not only wanted to learn about history, but be a part of it. In a time of incredible change, it can be easy to feel insignificant, yet history is written by the insignificant and the significant alike. I want to learn more about extreme life to inspire the next generation of scientists to believe in themselves, chase their dreams, and continue pushing forward the boundaries of discoveries. I also want to conduct global service, science-related or not, to connect with people and help local-communities hands on.

poster.title: Agnostic Life Finder: To Search for Extant Life in Martian Ice
poster.subtitle: Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference • Reykjavík, Iceland
poster.authors: Špaček, J.; Benner, S.; Temby, C.; Alpern, H.; Zeffren, J.; George, A.; Montaudon, E.; Rizzo, G.; Young, I.; Hunnewell, A.; Fuchs, L. (FfAME & NASA NIAC)
poster.abstract:
Presented at the Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference in Reykjavík, Iceland (July 2025), this poster summarizes laboratory validation of the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF). ALF is an instrument concept funded by NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) at the Foundation for Applied Molecular Evolution (FfAME) to detect extant Martian life in subsurface ice.

Grounded in the polyelectrolyte theory of the gene, ALF targets repeating backbone charges universal to genetic polymers. My primary engineering focus was designing, assembling, and testing three iterations of ALF's cylindrical flow-through ultrasonic sonicator to lyse resilient cells (including E. coli and S. cerevisiae) and shear genomic DNA to <500 bp without chemical buffers. Paired with a 7-channel electrodialysis stack (microfiltration, 4 kDa ultrafiltration, and Na+ exchange membranes), the system extracted 75% of DNA during overnight runs, concentrating it from 317.3 ng/µL to 903.4 ng/µL for downstream solid-state nanopore detection.

sections.label: 01. Rodwell Ice Extraction
sections.detail: Couples directly to Martian water-mining Rodwell systems planned for in-situ propellant electrolysis.

sections.label: 02. Flow-Through Sonicator
sections.detail: Custom cylindrical ultrasonic sonicator lyses E. coli & yeast cells and shears 200 ng/µL DNA to <500 bp.

sections.label: 03. 7-Channel Electrodialysis
sections.detail: Concentrated DNA from 317.3 ng/µL to 903.4 ng/µL (75% extraction) across MF, 4 kDa UF, and Na+ exchange membranes.

sections.label: 04. Nanopore Biosignatures
sections.detail: Routes concentrated polyanions and polycations to solid-state nanopores for single-molecule agnostic detection.

impressPaper.title: IMPRESS: A Planetary Penetrator Network for Astrobiology, Prospecting, and Exploration of Mars
impressPaper.citation: Spacek J, Alpern H, Dineen T, et al. Astrobiology. 2026;26(9):688–699.
impressPaper.summary:
Published as the September 2026 cover story of Astrobiology, the International Mars Prospecting Ride-Share System (IMPRESS) introduces a scalable, accessible, and low-cost mission architecture for distributed measurements on Mars, ahead of a sample return and human exploration. Instead of relying on expensive, infrequent soft landers and mechanical drills, IMPRESS deploys swarms of standardized ~2 kg planetary penetrators (IMPRESS-345, developed under a NASA TechLeap Prize award) that use descent kinetic energy to emplace a buried steel forebody connected via tether to a surface communications aftbody.

Because extant Martian life and habitable microenvironments may be patchily distributed, deploying dozens to thousands of probes across a landing ellipse provides spatial coverage, statistical replication, and tolerance to probe failure at an estimated delivery cost as low as ~$41,000 per probe. The paper also introduces a new thermal regime, which uses InSight regolith conductivity data (0.039 W m⁻¹K⁻¹) to show that dry Martian regolith acts as both impact shock absorber and thermal insulator. This would theoretically allow ~1 W of internal heat dissipation to keep buried instruments above 0°C (location dependent).
impressPaper.roleSummary: My Role — Second Author & Chief Operations Officer (COO) at IMPRESS Spaceworks Co.: Compiled the technical heritage review on NASA’s Deep Space 2 (DS2) Mars microprobes to evaluate experimental relevance for modern Mars astrobiology, analyzed candidate Martian landing sites and Hohmann transfer trajectories, manage company finances, serve as sole developer of impressmars.com, and support grants writing and scientific outreach.

publications: Spacek J, Alpern H, Dineen T, et al. IMPRESS: A Planetary Penetrator Network for Astrobiology, Prospecting, and Exploration of Mars. Astrobiology. 2026;26(9):688-699.

skills.contextTitle: Interdisciplinary Leadership Across NASA L’Space, UF Swamp Launch & Space Trek Academy

star.situation: Spaceflight and astrobiology missions require good coordination between scientists and aerospace engineers, who often operate on different schedules and prioritize different goals. I served as Project Manager and Chief Scientist in NASA L’Space, Payload Principal Investigator on the UF Swamp Launch Rocket Team, and Lead Biologist at the Florida Space Grant Consortium’s Space Trek Academy, continuously walking the tightrope between biology and engineering.
star.task: I wanted to prevent siloing between science and engineering sub-teams, so that engineers understood why they did what they did, and scientists (like me) understood what it required to get experiments functional. Doing so involved translating microbiological and astrobiological experimental goals into manufacturable flight hardware (in the case of Swamp Launch and Space Trek) and cohesive NASA proposals (for L'Space) under strict deadlines.
star.action: In NASA L’Space Mission Concept Academy, I scheduled and led cross-team meetings, managed a four-person science team, and guided the iteration of eleven spaceflight instruments from Pre-Phase A to Preliminary Design Review using Gantt charts and NASA risk matrices. On UF Swamp Launch, I formulated a ten-page proposal for an anaerobic B. subtilis payload launching to 10,000 ft, consulting UF faculty and collaborating closely with rocket engineers to help design a sterile syringe-based reagent injection system. At Space Trek Academy in Cape Canaveral, I coordinated with our flight team to prepare, launch, track, and recover hydrated and desiccated D. radiodurans cells on a 100,000 ft stratospheric weather balloon.
star.resolution: I successfully delivered NASA-reviewed mission architectures, Preliminary Design Reviews, and functional high-altitude biological payloads across all three initiatives, proving proactive communication can help transform complex scientific concepts into flight-ready hardware or solid proposals.

experiences.title: Reykjavík, Iceland: Frontiers in Astrobiology Conference & Waterfall Epistemology
experiences.subtitle: Presenting the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF) Poster & Redefining Purpose in Science
photoSlotLabels: Presenting the ALF Poster in Reykjavík
experiences.body:
Immediately after departing my cultural-exchange trip in Colombia in the summer 2025. I traveled to Reykjavík, Iceland to present my research on the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF) at the Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference. Surrounded by basalt columns, geothermal landscapes, and a mixed cohort early-career and senior astrobiologists from around the world, I presented my work on ultrasonic cell lysis and electrodialysis—a major milestone in my development as a Geology and Microbiology student.

After overcoming flight delays and reschedules, I made it to the conference, where I met fellow undergraduates from the US, Europe, and beyond, as well as graduate students and faculty. I spent my days listening to talks, discussing research with my peers, presenting my own findings, and socializing over coffee. I spent my nights exploring the city with my fellow researchers and locals. 

On the final day, we did our own version of the Golden Circle tour, exploring Iceland's unique volcanic geology, industry, and historical monuments. However, while my biggest takeaway from that day was certainly inspired by the natural beauty of the country, it was also founded in service. I remember staring at a remarkable waterfall and thinking that for all happiness academic achievement and success brought me, including this wonderful trip in Iceland, there was still a part of me that wanted to serve. I was inspired by the generosity and community warmth I had experienced in Bogotá and the friendliness I experienced from the people of Reykjavík. I still want to learn about extreme life in cold environments, because I think it paves the way for understanding any life that could exist beyond Earth, and those discoveries could have Earth-shattering ramifications. I was lucky to get flown out to Iceland to present my research and look at the beautiful natural landscape, but not many get that opportunity. Therefore, I not only want to discover new things, but make those discoveries more accessible through service so that other people become as enthusiastic about science as I am.

experiences.title: Bogotá & Suesca, Colombia: Cultural Immersion, History & Sandstone Crags
experiences.subtitle: Independent Immersion in the Colombian Andes, Language Practice & Historical Inquiry
experiences.body:
In the spring and summer of 2025, I traveled twice to Bogotá, Colombia, first in March for an international music and cultural festival, and again in June for a weeklong cultural immersion stay hosted by local friends I had connected with during my initial visit. Stepping outside the familiar structure of university travel or family trips, spending a week immersed in daily life challenged me to adapt quickly, communicate in Spanish, and engage with a new and unique culture. I'm from Miami, so it wasn't completely new, but living in Bogotá for a week was something species

Throughout my time, my days balanced outdoor exploration with everyday cultural exchange. I toured Bogotá, spent time in the countryside playing dominoes and sharing traditional home-cooked meals and Colombian coffee, learned how to play Tejo (think gunpowder cornhole), and traveled north to rock climb on the iconic sandstone cliffs of Suesca. Practicing conversational Spanish around the dinner table, discussing work, daily life, and global perspectives, strengthened my language confidence and adaptability beyond classroom study, though luckily my hosts were very fluent in English. Less fortunately, I could never quite manage to hit the gunpowder targets in Tejo.

As a History minor, I was equally drawn to Colombia’s modern political and social history. Through conversations with local students and visits to cultural landmarks in Bogotá—including the Gabriel García Márquez Cultural Center—I gained a much deeper understanding of Colombia’s decades-long internal conflict between government and guerrilla forces, the peace process of the past decade, and how competing socioeconomic perspectives continue to shape contemporary Colombian politics.

Ultimately, my time in Bogotá and Suesca made me more independent, open-minded, and globally aware. Experiencing such genuine cross-cultural hospitality prompted me to re-evaluate my own assumptions about community and professional purpose. The contrast between Colombia and Reykjavík, Iceland, where present my astrobiology research (Agnostic Life Finder sonicator)crystallized my goal of pairing rigorous scientific research with science communication and international volunteering that make a tangible, human-centered impact.

experiences.title: Reflection on One World: Photographs from a Shared Planet (Harn Museum)
experiences.subtitle: Harn Museum of Art Global Documentary Photography Reflection & Gallery
experiences.location: Harn Museum of Art, UF (Global Scope)
photoSlotLabels: Portrait of a Soldier: The 'thousand-yard stare' at ground level, prompting questions of trauma, compliance, and unseen history.
Community Portrait in Afghanistan: Civilians gathered around an outdoor studio backdrop, overlapping temporally with the soldiers deployed there.
Life Amidst Rubble in Palestine: Pigeons in flight and laundry drying above weathered concrete, evoking the enduring human lives behind headlines.
Lone Boy Atop a Freight Train: Looking down the length of a northbound train toward the U.S.–Mexico border into an uncertain horizon.
Elder in a UN Refugee Camp: Standing before a UNHCR tent with a gaze of unmistakable, defiant pride forged across a lifetime.
experiences.body:
I visited the Harn Museum mainly to explore the "One World" Global Photography exhibit. This exhibit appealed to me because of its personal focus on stories separated temporally and geographically. In times as divisive as these, I wanted to take a look at these photos to see what makes us human; not just the qualities valued by my culture, but the values innate to us as a species. One modern anxiety is the fear of being replaced by machines. Through this exhibit, I wanted to see if there was such a thing as the "indomitable human spirit," or if it is just wishful thinking by people wanting to feel important.

Each photo was unique, but there were of course some that especially stood out to me. One was a large portrait of a soldier with his head on the side of a table. His wide eyes were clear, giving the classic "thousand-yard stare", but I wonder if what he really felt in that moment was confusion, as he was complying with an odd request and likely had a camera right in his face. Nevertheless, it was an interesting photo, as he had most definitely seen things. Some of the other photos showed crowds of civilians in Afghanistan, and I wondered if they had ever met this soldier.

This was the beginning of the connections I made between the pieces, and between the history shown within them and the events going on today. For example, a 2006 photograph showed a Palestinian family amidst the rubble of their former home. I realized the kids from that era were now adults, and the parents were now old. I wondered what lives they had lived since then and if they were still alive. Another striking photograph showed a lone boy on the top of a train, likely aiming to cross the US-Mexico border. I wondered if he had made it, and if he was still here, or deported. It is one thing to hear about death and deportation on the news, but it is another thing to look into the eyes of the people affected by that news.

These people were more than just victims though. I saw an old man in a UN refugee camp. When I looked at him, I saw a strong sense of defiant pride, resonating from every wrinkle on his face. I knew he had lived a life four times as long as mine, and that there was so much more to him than that one emotion, and yet in that image, that pride was all I could see. To me, that is how he would be remembered. Another photo that struck me was a lone man standing in front of several armored cars and armed personnel, protesting the Dakota Access Pipeline which was being built on Reservation land. I wondered how the men thought of themselves, facing a lone man with all that protection. How could they not see themselves as cowards? If you are armed facing the unarmed and courageous, how can you still think you are right? In the picture, it seems obvious, but maybe I'm oversimplifying.

Anyways, I still don't know if there is an indomitable human spirit, but I know that there is a shared human world. These photos aren't isolated—they overlap each other and my own life. Many of the conflicts and situations shown in the photos continue to this day. New photos are being taken, capturing flashes of lives just as rich as mine. However, I will never meet these people, and I will never be able to see their lives, only these brief flashes. If anything, this makes me feel isolated. We're all connected, and yet I'm exposed to a tiny fraction of it all, and I worry about a lot of stupid things that only affect me. Viewing this exhibit motivates me to travel the world and gain new perspectives and hopefully make a tangible difference in the lives of others.

experiences.title: Cross-Cultural Symposia: Brazilian History, Populist Discourse & South African Hydrology
experiences.subtitle: Synthesizing Two Latin American Studies Coloquios & the Center for African Studies Baraza
experiences.body:
Attending three interdisciplinary lectures across UF’s Center for Latin American Studies (Coloquios) and Center for African Studies (Baraza) allowed me to connect my History minor with my Geology and Microbiology majors across both the South Atlantic and Southern Africa.

In the first Coloquio, "Rethinking Human Rights through the African Diaspora: A Brazilian Perspective," Dr. Sant’Ana examined the protracted dismantling of slavery in Brazil—the last Latin American nation to abolish the institution in 1888. While the 1871 Law of the Free Womb declared children born to enslaved mothers legally free, Dr. Sant’Ana highlighted how structural economic dependence kept many bound to former masters, even as autonomous quilombo settlements fostered enduring anti-slavery thought and four pioneering Afro-Brazilian thinkers challenged the persistence of a post-abolition racial caste system. A second Coloquio by Dr. Luz, "The People in the Kaleidoscope: Bolsonarist Discourse in Light of Contemporary Populist Theories," traced how modern Brazilian politics leverages outsider framing, social media mobilization, and an "us versus elites" narrative. Comparing Brazil’s 2018 election with populist currents in the United States showed me that populism is ultimately an instrument—one that can voice legitimate grievances of the marginalized, yet also risks stripping away nuance when voters are not critical of who wields it.

Complementing these historical and political perspectives, the Center for African Studies Baraza by Dr. Tatenda Dalu (Stellenbosch University), "Day Zero Lessons: Invasive Alien Plants as Water–Fire Risk Multipliers," bridged my geoscience and biology training in the context of Cape Town, South Africa. Dr. Dalu demonstrated how invasive species impose over $400 billion in global economic costs and severely deplete South African water reservoirs when high-transpiration trees like invasive pines and Red Gum establish along watersheds. Learning how targeted removal of invasive pines and restoration of native fynbos bush measurably recovers reservoir levels underscored how hydrogeology, plant ecology, and public policy must work together to safeguard vulnerable communities.

pillars.heading: I. Stepping Outside the Geographic & Disciplinary Bubble
pillars.body: When I began my journey at the University of Florida as a Geology and Microbiology double major, it was easy to treat science as a self-contained puzzle of rocks, water tables, and microbes. Adding a History minor and engaging with the International Scholars Program challenged me to look up from the microscope. Attending colloquia on Afro-Brazilian quilombos and post-1888 abolition, analyzing populist rhetoric in Brazil alongside U.S. political currents, and learning how invasive pines threaten South African water reservoirs taught me that ecological and historical systems are deeply intertwined. Every landscape carries a human memory, and every environmental crisis carries a human cost.

pillars.heading: II. Two Moments of Clarity: Bogotá’s Table & Reykjavík’s Waterfall
pillars.body: The contrast between my week in Bogotá, Colombia, and my research conference in Reykjavík, Iceland, became the defining inflection point of my undergraduate years. In Colombia, local hosts welcomed me into their home with extraordinary warmth. Over home-cooked meals, Colombian coffee, games of dominoes, rock climbing in Suesca, and candid conversations about Colombia’s history, I saw how human generosity dissolves cultural guardedness. Weeks later, standing before a waterfall in Iceland after presenting my scientific research, I thought about academia. I loved the rigor of research, yet looking at that waterfall, I realized that even the most profound scientific discoveries would feel hollow to me without a human element.

pillars.heading: III. Now What? Planetary Exploration, Astrobiology & Global Service
pillars.body: As I graduate from UF, the question of 'Now What?' has a clear answer. Just as the photographs in the Harn Museum’s 'One World' exhibit reminded me that we inhabit a single shared human world, my experiences in Colombia and Iceland shaped my commitment to pair frontier astrobiology—at IMPRESS Spaceworks Co. and in my future PhD studying cold-loving microbes in Antarctica—with science communication and international volunteering that connect directly with communities around the globe.
